docs.metricsIntro: Every figure in the app comes from a specific formula, and every one of them has a limit. Here are both.
docs.title: Documentation
docs.intro: How training is organised in the app, and what each term means. The first four — session, cycle, stage and program — nest inside one another: each groups the one before it.

sections.title: Session
points: One training day: the exercises you do in one go.
Within the cycle they're named in order: A, B, C…
The letter tells you when it comes up, not what it is: reorder them and they're reassigned.

sections.title: Cycle
points: The group of sessions that repeats over and over. In training theory, the microcycle.
If you train A, B and C, the cycle is A-B-C; finish it and it starts again at A.
It usually matches the days you train in a week.
It moves on once you complete ALL of its sessions, not when the week ends.
Order doesn't matter, and repeating a session doesn't count twice.

sections.title: Stage
points: A stretch of the program with one goal: build volume, gain strength, peak. In training theory, the mesocycle.
You build it from a cycle and the number of times you want to repeat it.
Four cycles of A-B-C are A-B-C, A-B-C, A-B-C, A-B-C.
Once you complete them the app tells you, but it never jumps to the next one on its own.
Stages are what let a program evolve instead of repeating the same thing forever.

sections.title: Program
points: The complete plan from start to finish: all of its stages together. In training theory, the macrocycle.
Only one is active at a time.
The rest are archived and you can bring them back whenever you want.

sections.title: Block
points: Conditioning work driven by the clock instead of sets.
AMRAP: most rounds in a time cap.
EMOM: one task per minute.
For time: a fixed amount of work, as fast as possible.

sections.title: Superset
points: Two or more exercises chained with no rest between them.
The rest is taken after the last one in the chain.

sections.title: Dropset
points: Extra sets after the last working set, dropping the weight without resting.
They add volume.
They don't count towards PRs or progression.

sections.title: Progression
points: The rule that sets the weight for your next session.
Automatic: goes up when you hit the target.
Fixed: always the same increment.
Submaximal: a percentage of your max.

sections.title: RPE
points: Perceived effort from 1 to 10.
How many reps you'd have left in the tank.
RPE 8 means roughly 2 reps in reserve.

sections.title: 1RM
points: Your estimated maximum for a single rep.
It isn't measured by lifting it: it's calculated from your sets.

sections.title: PR
points: A personal record on an exercise.
More weight, more reps at the same weight, or more volume than in any previous session.

loadOverTime.name: Load over time
loadOverTime.what: Each bar is one day's load. The two lines are the average of the last 7 days (lime) and the last 28 (blue), which show the overall shape beneath the day-to-day noise.
loadOverTime.read: When the 7-day line runs above the 28-day one you are building more load than usual; when it drops below, you are deloading. Frequent crossings are a sign of healthy alternation. What's worth watching is a large, sustained gap.

effortVsLoad.name: Effort vs load
effortVsLoad.what: Two weekly lines: the work you do (external load) and what it costs you (effort). They come in different units, so both are rescaled to base 100 to make them comparable.
effortVsLoad.read: What matters is whether they separate, not where they sit. More work at the same cost means you are adapting. The same work costing more is accumulated fatigue. Both rising is a hard block, and both falling is a deload.

performance.name: Performance
performance.what: How your average estimated 1RM evolves over the period, with 100 at your starting point.
performance.read: This is the system's output: load is what you put in, this is what comes out. Rising here with steady load is the clearest sign the training is working. Falling while load rises usually warns of a plateau.

strainWeekly.name: Strain by week
strainWeekly.what: Each week's accumulated stress, one bar per week. Weeks with fewer than 3 sessions appear as an outline: you trained, but there is no reliable value to draw.
strainWeekly.read: The shape rules, not the exact height. Three or four weeks rising and then a drop is a healthy mesocycle. Rising without ever dropping is what to watch for.

muscleGroups.name: Sets per group
muscleGroups.what: The last 7 days' sets split by muscle group, with two marks showing the reference range.
muscleGroups.read: Look for gaps, not perfection. A group at zero or well below the range for several weeks in a row is what's actionable. Going over the top isn't bad in itself if you recover well.

e1rm.name: Estimated 1RM
e1rm.what: Estimates the heaviest weight you could lift once, without having to actually attempt it. It lets you track progress on an exercise even when your rep counts change week to week.
e1rm.rules: If you log RPE, the reps you had left in reserve (10 − RPE) are estimated and added to the reps performed before applying the formula: a set at RPE 8 is calculated as if you had done two more reps.
e1rm.caveat: This is Epley's formula, an estimate and not a measurement. Sets above {{maxReps}} reps are ignored because beyond that it overestimates noticeably.

pr.name: Personal record (PR)
pr.what: Flags the sessions where you beat your previous best on an exercise.
pr.formula: estimated 1RM is compared; if it can't be computed, top weight; and failing that, bodyweight reps
pr.rules: The comparison runs against your whole previous history, not just the last session. The first time you do an exercise sets your initial reference, so it doesn't count as a record. One record is flagged per exercise and session: the first on that ladder.
pr.caveat: Because it leans on the estimated 1RM, it inherits its margin of error: a narrow record may come from the estimate rather than from a real improvement.

performanceIndex.name: Performance
performanceIndex.what: Sums up in a single number how your estimated performance has evolved across every exercise in the period. It tells you whether the training is turning into results.
performanceIndex.formula: average of (each exercise's estimated 1RM ÷ its initial value) × 100
performanceIndex.rules: For each week the best estimated 1RM from the 4 previous weeks is used, not that week alone, so a deload doesn't show up as lost performance. An exercise only counts if it has an initial value and at least one later week with data. The indexes are averaged, not the kilos.
performanceIndex.caveat: This is estimated performance, not measured strength: it rests entirely on the estimated 1RM. Changing exercises mid-period moves the number even if your performance doesn't change.

loadTrend.name: Improvement
loadTrend.what: Tells you whether the weights you move are going up or down on average during the period, combining all your exercises into one percentage.
loadTrend.formula: trend line (linear regression) over each exercise's sessions; the percentage is the change between its ends, averaged across exercises
loadTrend.rules: Every exercise carries the same weight in the average, regardless of how many sessions it has.
loadTrend.caveat: It's the slope of a line fitted to all your sessions, not the difference between the first and the last. A brand-new exercise with few points can move the result more than it should.

lastSessionDelta.name: Difference from previous session
lastSessionDelta.what: Compares your last session with the previous one of the same type so you can see at a glance whether you went up or down.
lastSessionDelta.rules: In History this difference is computed on volume and compares against the previous run of that same session, not the chronologically previous one.
lastSessionDelta.caveat: It's only two sessions: one bad day, or one unusually good one, moves the result entirely.

volume.name: Volume
volume.what: Adds up the total kilos you moved in a session. Useful for comparing the amount of work between similar sessions.
volume.formula: volume = sum of (weight × reps) over every logged set
volume.caveat: Bodyweight exercises count as 0 kg of volume because they have no external weight logged. A session of pull-ups and dips can show very little volume even if it was hard.

setsDonePlanned.name: Sets done and planned
setsDonePlanned.what: Shows how many sets you logged versus how many the session had, so you can see whether you finished it.
setsDonePlanned.formula: done = sets with logged data or ticked · planned = sum of the template's sets
setsDonePlanned.rules: Planned sets are frozen when the session is saved. An exercise you skip disappears from the saved session, but its sets still count as planned: that's what makes the gap visible.
setsDonePlanned.caveat: A set ticked without data counts as done exactly like one with weight and reps.

volumeTrend.name: Volume (Progress tab)
volumeTrend.what: Compares the volume of the period's first session with that of the last one.
volumeTrend.formula: (last session's volume − first session's volume) ÷ first session's volume × 100
volumeTrend.caveat: It is not a trend line: it's two points. An unusual session at either end changes the result completely.

muscleGroupSets.name: Sets per muscle group
muscleGroupSets.what: Splits the last 7 days' sets across muscle groups, so you can spot one falling behind.
muscleGroupSets.formula: sum of the sets of the exercises whose primary muscle group is that one
muscleGroupSets.rules: It counts direct volume: a bench press adds to chest and gives nothing to triceps or shoulders. A dropset counts as a single set. Groups you trained in the 4 previous weeks but not in the last 7 days show as zero instead of disappearing.
muscleGroupSets.caveat: The {{min}} to {{max}} set reference range is a hypertrophy guideline and depends on your goal. By ignoring indirect volume, groups you mostly work as secondary come out lower than you actually train them.

sessionLoad.name: Session load
sessionLoad.what: Sums up in one number how much a session cost you, combining its duration with how hard it felt. It's the basis of the whole Load tab.
sessionLoad.rules: Without answering the RPE there is no load: the session leaves a gap in the charts, never a zero. Conditioning blocks contribute {{blockFactor}} units per active second.
sessionLoad.caveat: This is Foster's sRPE method. The number means nothing on its own: it only makes sense compared to your own sessions. The block factor is hand-tuned and is the least reliable part of the calculation.

sessionMinutes.name: Session minutes
sessionMinutes.what: This is the duration used to compute the session load.
sessionMinutes.formula: minutes = real elapsed time, limited to between half and double the estimated duration
sessionMinutes.rules: Real time runs from when you start the session until you save it. The limit stops a session left open for several hours from multiplying your load.
sessionMinutes.caveat: That time includes rests, pauses and the phone in your pocket. Since sets don't record when you did them, there's no measure of genuinely active time.

externalLoad.name: External load
externalLoad.what: Measures the work you did as reps weighted by how close to your max they were. It lets you compare sessions made of different exercises.
externalLoad.formula: external load = sum of reps × (weight ÷ reference 1RM)
externalLoad.rules: The reference 1RM is your best estimated 1RM from the 6 weeks before that session, frozen by date so today's record can't rewrite your history. Bodyweight exercises need your logged body weight; isometrics and timed sets don't count, as they have no reps.
externalLoad.caveat: It's not tonnage: it normalises by your current capacity, so a curl set and a squat set at the same relative intensity contribute a similar load. Because it depends on the estimated 1RM, it inherits its margin of error.

movingAverage.name: 7 and 28 day averages
movingAverage.what: These are the smooth lines on the load chart: your usual load over the last week and the last month. They show the overall shape above the day-to-day noise.
movingAverage.formula: average daily load over the last 7 (or 28) days, counting rest days as 0
movingAverage.rules: Until you have 28 days of history it averages whatever days exist, rather than leaving the line unstarted. Days you trained without answering the RPE are left out of the average instead of counting as zero: unknown is not rest.
movingAverage.caveat: A moving average smooths, but it also lags: a real change in load takes a few days to show up in the line.

loadState.name: Load state
loadState.what: Sums up whether you're building load, holding steady, or deloading.
loadState.formula: 7-day average ÷ 28-day average → below 0.8 deload · 0.8 to 1.3 steady · above 1.3 building
loadState.rules: It's shown as a state and not as a number on purpose.
loadState.caveat: This is the acute/chronic ratio. The numeric version carries known mathematical artefacts and its risk thresholds don't replicate consistently across studies, so treat it as guidance rather than a traffic light.

monotony.name: Monotony
monotony.what: Indicates whether you repeat the same load day after day without variation, a pattern linked to worse recovery. The LOWER the better: it means you alternate hard days with easy ones.
monotony.formula: monotony = average daily load ÷ its standard deviation, over 7 days
monotony.rules: Rest days count as 0, as the original method defines. It's hidden when the week has fewer than {{minSessions}} sessions. Above {{high}} it's flagged as high; below {{moderate}}, as low.
monotony.caveat: With one or two sessions in the week, rest days dominate the deviation and the number stops meaning anything: that's why it's hidden rather than shown in green.

strain.name: Strain
strain.what: Sums up the week's accumulated stress by combining how much load you did with how little you varied it.
strain.formula: strain = the week's total load × monotony
strain.rules: It's shown against your own average of the 4 previous weeks. It's hidden when the week has fewer than {{minSessions}} sessions, same as monotony.
strain.caveat: There is no universal strain threshold, so it's never shown with fixed colours or an alarm value: it only makes sense against your own history.

indexed100.name: Base 100
indexed100.what: The rescaling that lets two quantities with different units be drawn together, such as external load and effort.
indexed100.formula: value ÷ first value of the period × 100
indexed100.rules: The 100 corresponds to the start of the selected period, so it changes when you move the selector.
indexed100.caveat: If the period's first week was unusual — a deload, say — it shifts the whole series upwards.

loadHeatmap.name: Calendar heatmap
loadHeatmap.what: Shades each calendar day by that session's load, so you can spot your hard days and your streaks at a glance.
loadHeatmap.formula: four steps spread by quartiles of your own daily load
loadHeatmap.rules: The cuts are computed over your whole history, not the visible month, so they mean the same thing as you move between months. A day trained without answering the RPE is drawn as an outline with no fill, because there's no load to represent.
loadHeatmap.caveat: The colour ranks your days against each other, not against an absolute value: there will always be dark and light days even if you train very uniformly.

sessionCount.name: Sessions
sessionCount.what: Counts the sessions you completed within the selected period. It tells you whether you are keeping the pace.
sessionCount.formula: number of sessions saved within the period
sessionCount.rules: It follows the period selector and the program filter. The “this week” subtitle, however, always counts the current calendar week, Monday to Sunday, regardless of the period selected.
sessionCount.caveat: It counts sessions, not their size: a ten-minute warm-up and a two-hour session add up the same.

weekSessions.name: Sessions (last 7 days)
weekSessions.what: How many times you have trained in the last 7 days. It sits next to load because it is what gives load meaning: 2,400 of load does not mean the same coming from 3 sessions as from 5.
weekSessions.formula: number of sessions saved in the last 7 days
weekSessions.rules: It is a rolling 7-day window, not the calendar week: on a Monday morning the calendar week is nearly empty and the figure would be useless. The subtitle is your average over the 4 previous weeks, to tell whether this week is normal for you. It is also the count that decides whether monotony and strain are shown or hidden.
weekSessions.caveat: It counts sessions, not their size: a ten-minute warm-up and a two-hour session add up the same. Not to be confused with the “Sessions” card in Progress, which counts the selected period.

progressionChip.name: Progression suggestion
progressionChip.what: The go up, hold or back off hint shown on each exercise during a workout, based on how the last one went.
progressionChip.formula: qualifying sets ÷ target sets, crossed with the rep range and with RPE if you log it
progressionChip.rules: A qualifying set is one that reached the exercise's minimum reps (or time); a set ticked as done without data also counts. With RPE evaluation mode, going up additionally requires the average RPE to stay under the ceiling you set.
progressionChip.caveat: It only looks at your last session of that exercise, not your progression over time. It's a suggestion: ignoring it affects nothing else.

estimatedDuration.name: Estimated duration
estimatedDuration.what: Works out how long a session will take before you do it, so you can fit it to the time you have.
estimatedDuration.formula: sets × (35 s + rest) + 180 s per exercise + 480 s general warm-up
estimatedDuration.rules: The 180 seconds per exercise cover the changeover: finding the machine, loading the bar, adjusting. In supersets each member's full rest is counted.
estimatedDuration.caveat: It's a model, not a measurement: it assumes you keep the configured rests and doesn't know if you linger between sets. It overestimates supersets slightly.

warmupWeight.name: Warm-up weights
warmupWeight.what: Suggests the weights for your ramp-up sets from the day's working weight.
warmupWeight.formula: weight = percentage of the day's working weight, rounded to 2.5 kg
warmupWeight.rules: The working weight comes from the trainer's prescription or, failing that, your heaviest set last time. With neither, the pills stay empty until you type your first weight. They aren't saved to your history.
warmupWeight.caveat: They're guidance: the percentage doesn't distinguish between exercises and doesn't know how you feel that day.

blockDelta.name: Block comparison
blockDelta.what: Tells you whether you improved on the last time you did that same conditioning block.
blockDelta.formula: AMRAP: rounds and reps · EMOM: intervals completed · For time: time
blockDelta.rules: In for-time blocks less time is better, so the sign is inverted compared to the other two formats. It compares against the previous run of the same session, not your best ever result.
blockDelta.caveat: Blocks don't record the weight used, so two identical results with different loads are compared as if they were equivalent.

stageProgress.name: Stage progress
stageProgress.what: Counts how many weeks of the stage you've completed, so you know how far you are from moving on.
stageProgress.formula: one week = one full pass through every distinct session of the cycle
stageProgress.rules: Repeating a session doesn't count twice: you have to go through all the cycle's sessions. The counter belongs to the client and is replicated to the trainer; it isn't derived from the history.
stageProgress.caveat: It's not a calendar week: if you train A-B-C over five days, that's your week. That's why this counter and the Load tab's weeks can disagree.

adherence.name: Adherence
adherence.what: Flags which clients are drifting away from the frequency their program asks for. It measures drop-off risk from time without training, not the percentage of sessions completed.
adherence.formula: days since the last session ÷ (7 ÷ sessions per week) → up to 2 on track · above 4 at risk
adherence.rules: The threshold scales with the program's frequency, so it's fair across clients training 2 or 5 days a week. The weekly average uses the 4 complete previous weeks, excluding the one in progress, so a Monday morning doesn't look like a slowdown. Pausing a client silences adherence.
adherence.caveat: It's not a completion percentage: a client who trains today looks fine even if they'd been off for three weeks. It measures how long they've gone without training relative to what they should, not their cumulative record.

trainer.title: Trainer
trainer.connectedSub: They send you programs and see the sessions you complete from them.
trainer.pendingSub: Your last session hasn't reached them yet. It retries when you open the app, or you can retry now.
trainer.offSub: If you train on your own you don't need this. Connect only if a trainer writes your programs.
trainer.rowProgramSub: If they update it, the app tells you and you choose when to switch.
trainer.rowProgramNoneSub: They haven't sent you a program yet.
trainer.rowLastUploadSub: Sent on its own after every session.
trainer.rowLastUploadFailed: Failed on {{when}}. It will retry automatically.
trainer.rowAccessGoogleSub: You can restore the connection on another phone without asking your trainer for anything.
trainer.rowAccessCode: You sign in with a code
trainer.rowAccessCodeSub: The code never expires or changes: it's always the same one. Save it so you can get back in if you change phones or reinstall the app.
trainer.sharedBody: The sessions you complete from the programs they send you, plus any free sessions you log after you connected.
trainer.notSharedBody: Programs you built yourself, or anything you trained before connecting.
trainer.retrySub: Try to send your history right now.
trainer.linkGoogleSub: So you don't depend on the code if you change phones or reinstall.
trainer.changeSub: You'll enter the new trainer's code. The current program is archived and theirs arrives instead.
trainer.disconnectSub: You stop sending sessions. Their program is archived and your previous one comes back. Same code to come back.
trainer.disconnectBody: You'll stop sending them your sessions. Their program will be archived and your previous one restored, if you had one. You can reconnect later with the same code.
trainer.how1Sub: It lands in the app and you train with it like any other.
trainer.how2Title: Your sessions reach them on their own
trainer.how2Sub: After every session the log is sent so they can see how you're doing.
trainer.how3Sub: Eight characters like XK7M-2P4T, given to you by your trainer. It's always the same one, so save it: you'll need it if you reinstall the app.
trainer.socialCtaHint: Only if you were connected before and linked an account: it restores the connection without typing the code again.
trainer.socialLead: Sign in with the account you linked and we'll restore your connection with the trainer.
trainer.socialSearching: Looking for the linked trainer connection…
trainer.socialNoSlot: That account has no saved connection. Ask your trainer for the code.
trainer.expoGoNote: Signing in doesn't work in Expo Go. Try the installed app.
trainer.errNoIdToken: The account identity wasn't returned. Try again.
trainer.codeLead: Type the code your trainer gave you. It's eight characters like XK7M-2P4T; the dash is added for you.
trainer.codeAlreadyLinked: You're already connected to a trainer. Continuing disconnects you from them and connects you to this one.
trainer.codeSlotOccupied: This slot is already taken by a device. If that's you and you reinstalled the app, your trainer needs to issue you a new code — your history is kept.
trainer.errSlotOccupied: This slot is already taken. Ask your trainer to issue you a new code — you won't lose your history.
trainer.errCodeNotFound: Code not found. Check that you typed it correctly.
trainer.codeHistoryProgramSub: The trainer's program is imported. The history on this phone doesn't change.
trainer.codeHistoryMergeSub: Also restores the history your trainer has stored. Repeated sessions aren't duplicated.
trainer.codeImplies1: Your current program is archived and your trainer's is loaded.
trainer.codeImplies2: Your trainer will see the sessions you complete from their programs.
trainer.codeImplies3: If they change the program, the app tells you and you choose when to switch.
trainer.codeImplies4: Your previous history isn't deleted, and isn't sent to them.
trainer.linkLead: Link an account to restore the connection with your trainer on another phone without asking them for the code again.
trainer.linkImplies1: Your trainer connection and your history stay exactly as they are.
trainer.linkImplies2: On another phone, just sign in with the same account.
trainer.linkImplies3: You won't have to keep any code.
trainer.linkErrBody: Couldn't link the account. Try again.

sync.title: Sync
sync.selectLead: Choose how the app should keep your clients. You can change this later.
sync.modeGoogleDesc: Your clients are tied to your account. There's no code to keep: you sign in with Google and that's it.
sync.modeAppleDesc: Same as Google, but with your Apple ID. You can hide your email and still recover the account.
sync.modeCodeDesc: The app creates a 12-character code. Everything works the same, but that code is your only key.
sync.modeCodeWarn: Keeping it is on you: without that code the account can't be recovered.
sync.modeOfflineDesc: Nothing leaves this phone. You share programs and history by exporting and importing files by hand.
sync.onlyInstalled: Installed app only, not Expo Go.
sync.warnCodeExists: You already have a code. Creating another one stops your current clients from syncing with it.
sync.warnUpgrade: Your current clients move to your account on their own.
sync.nameHint: This is the name your clients see on the programs you send them.
sync.reauthGoogleLink: Sign in with a different Google account →
sync.statusSub: With your personal code. Keep it: it's what gives the account back if you change phones.
sync.reauthHint: Use it if the app stopped recognising you: it signs in again with the code you already have.
sync.revealLead: This is your code. Copy it and keep it somewhere safe: it's the only way to recover the account.
sync.revealWarn: If you lose the phone and don't have the code, the account and the sync with your clients can't be recovered.
sync.recoveryLink: Already have a code? Recover account →
sync.reauthLink: Sign in again with another code →
sync.recoveryLead: Type your trainer code to get your clients back. It's twelve characters; the dashes are added for you.
sync.switchBody: The current account will be signed out. Your clients stay on this phone, but stop syncing until you sign in again.
sync.switchUpgradeBody: Your current clients move to your account on their own and you stop depending on the code.
sync.errNoIdToken: The account identity wasn't returned. Try again.
sync.errReconnectBody: Check your code and try again.

drive.title: Drive backup
drive.offSub: Your data lives only on this phone. If you lose it or reinstall the app, it goes with it.
drive.activeSubNever: No backup has been saved yet.
drive.reconnectSub: Google expired the permission. Reconnect the account to keep saving backups.
drive.how1Sub: Programs, history, your own exercises, settings, and also your clients and session templates, in a "Forma Backups" folder on your Google Drive.
drive.how2Sub: The app can only see the files it creates itself; the rest of your Drive is invisible to it.
drive.how3Sub: Each backup is a file with its date. Past 30, the oldest ones are deleted automatically.
drive.expoGoNote: Google sign-in doesn't work in Expo Go. Try the installed app (EAS build).
drive.freqSessionSub: Recommended: the backup is always current and needs no background permissions.
drive.freqDailySub: In the background, even if you don't train that day.
drive.freqWeeklySub: In the background, even if you don't train that week.
drive.freqMonthlySub: In the background, even if you don't train that month.
drive.nameHint: The date is added automatically, so you can tell your backups apart in Drive.
drive.backupNowSub: Don't wait for the next session.
drive.deleteAllSub: They're deleted from your Drive and can't be recovered.
drive.disconnectSub: No new backups are saved. The ones already in Drive are kept.
drive.backupsHint: Tap a backup to restore it on this phone.
drive.backupsEmpty: There are no backups in your Drive yet.
drive.backupsNeedConnect: Connect your Google account in the Settings tab to see your backups.
drive.backupsLoadFailed: Couldn't reach your Drive. Pull down to try again.
drive.backupsNeedReconnect: Your Google session expired, so we couldn't check your Drive. Reconnect in the Settings tab — your backups are still there.
drive.errExpiredBody: Reconnect your Google account to keep saving backups.
drive.restoreBody: Everything you have in the app right now (programs, history and settings) is replaced by what was in the backup from {{when}}. This can't be undone.
drive.deleteAllBody: They'll be deleted from your Google Drive and can't be recovered. The app stays connected and will save new ones.
drive.disconnectBody: No new backups will be saved. The backups already in your Drive are kept and you can reconnect whenever you want.

home.stageLockedText: You've finished {{current}}. The next one, {{next}}, is locked — your trainer has to open it.
home.stageLockedHint: In the meantime you can keep training this stage.
home.startOutOfOrderDesc: It's not the next session in your cycle.

archiveModal.title: Archive program
archiveModal.desc: It will be saved in archives. You can restore it later.
archiveModal.keepHistoryDesc: The program is archived, session history is preserved
archiveModal.clearHistoryDesc: All recorded sessions for this program will be deleted

workout.discardConfirm: Discard current session? All entered data will be lost.
workout.notesPlaceholder: Note how the session went, feelings, adjustments for next time...
workout.notesSavedWith: Saved with the session when you press SAVE SESSION.
workout.clientNotePlaceholder: Note for your trainer (discomfort, how it felt…)

warmup.noReference: Weights are calculated once you enter your first work weight

freeSession.infoText: One-off session — saved to your history and linked to the active program, but doesn't affect progress or your week counter.

emomModeDesc.all: Every interval you do all the movements and rest for whatever is left.
emomModeDesc.rotate: One exercise per interval. They rotate automatically.

formatDesc.amrap: As many rounds as possible within a set time.
formatDesc.emom: A fixed interval that repeats; each interval has its own work.
formatDesc.for_time: Complete every round as fast as you can.

blocks.cancelConfirm: Cancel the block? Progress will be lost.
blocks.partialHint: When time is up you can adjust the partial round
blocks.failHint: Tap an interval to mark it as failed
blocks.timeUp: Time! Adjust your score and finish
blocks.timeUpEmom: Time! Mark any misses and finish

summary.amrapSub_other: Go through the {{count}} movements as many times as you can

beginner.label: Beginner
beginner.description: Less than 1 year training or returning after a long break.
beginner.detail: Machine-guided exercises, basic bodyweight and dumbbell patterns. Simple and safe progression.

intermediate.label: Intermediate
intermediate.detail: Dumbbells, cables, kettlebell and technical bodyweight exercises like pull-ups or dips. Double progression.

advanced.label: Advanced
advanced.description: 3+ years with solid technique in free movements.
advanced.detail: Barbell, weighted exercises, periodization. Requires good technique in squat, deadlift and press.

standard.label: Standard
standard.description: Hypertrophy and general strength. The most complete and versatile approach.
standard.detail: Covers all movement patterns with the best exercises for each goal.

calisthenics.label: Calisthenics / Functional
calisthenics.description: Bodyweight, grip and core. With transfer to sports and aerial disciplines.
calisthenics.detail: Pull-ups, dips, L-sit, hollow body. Relative strength and body control.

glutes_legs.label: Legs & Glutes
glutes_legs.description: Maximum emphasis on glutes, hamstrings and legs. Popular in female programs.
glutes_legs.detail: Hip thrust, Romanian deadlift, leg press and squat variations as central exercises.

strength.label: Strength / Powerlifting
strength.description: Move more weight. Squat, deadlift and press as the core.
strength.detail: 3–6 rep ranges, long rests and load progression as priority.

full_body.label: Full Body
full_body.description: All muscle groups in each session. 2–6 days.

upper_lower.label: Upper / Lower
upper_lower.description: Upper body one day, lower the next. 2 distinct sessions.

push_pull_legs.label: Push / Pull / Legs
push_pull_legs.description: One push day, one pull day, one legs day. 3 sessions.

hypertrophy.label: Hypertrophy
hypertrophy.description: Build muscle mass. 8–12 reps per set.

strength.label: Strength
strength.description: Move more weight. 5–8 reps, long rests.

bodyweight.label: Bodyweight only
bodyweight.description: No equipment — exercises using just your body.

none.label: No limitations
none.description: I can do any exercise without restrictions.

shoulder.label: Shoulder / Trapezius
shoulder.description: Discomfort in shoulder, rotator cuff or trapezius.

lower_back.label: Lower back
lower_back.description: Problems in the lower back area.

double_progression.label: Double progression
double_progression.description: Reach max reps → increase weight → return to min. The most common.

linear.label: Linear progression
linear.description: Add a fixed weight each session. Classic in strength programs like Starting Strength.

reps_progression.label: Rep progression
reps_progression.description: Weight stays the same, only reps increase each session.

upperLowerOptions.2sessionsDesc: A (upper) + B (lower). Simpler, repeat the cycle.
upperLowerOptions.4sessionsDesc: A1 + B1 + A2 + B2. More exercise variety per cycle.

deleteAccount.title: Delete account
deleteAccount.lead: Your account and everything stored in it will be deleted from the server. This can't be undone.
deleteAccount.noAccount: There's no account to delete: this app is in offline mode and nothing of yours leaves this phone. To start over, uninstall the app.
deleteAccount.implTrainer: Your clients stop syncing: they lose the program you sent them and their code stops working.
deleteAccount.implClient: You stop being connected to your trainer, and the history they had of you is deleted.
deleteAccount.implIrreversible: There's no way to get it back. Not with your code, not by signing in again with Google or Apple.
deleteAccount.staysLocal: Your history, programs and exercises on this phone stay as they are. The app keeps working without an account.
deleteAccount.staysPro: If you have Pro you keep it: the purchase belongs to your Apple or Google Play account, not this one. Restore it with "Restore purchases".
